newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong punters in grip of red-chip fever.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong punters in grip of red-chip fever.

text.p: Hong Kong remained gripped by red-chip fever on Thursday as enthusiasts for China-related shares listed in the territory jostled for Beijing Enterprises Holdings Ltd's initial public offering.

The offering by the well-connected Beijing-based conglomerate has sparked huge demand from retail investors with thousands of punters rushing to snap up application forms before Friday's deadline to subscribe to the issue.
"They may not necessarily know what its business is...but they know that it is a company controlled by the Beijing municipal government," said Percy Au-Young, director of research of DBS Securities.

Beijing Enterprises, involved in retail, infrastructure and other businesses, is offering 150 million H-shares at HK$12.48 each. Ten percent of the issue is earmarked for public offering in Hong Kong and 90 percent for international placement.
The queue for application forms shortened on Thursday after the issue's sponsor rushed to print up more to meet demand.

"It appeared that demand has been lagging. We are not going to print more...demand has been tapering off considerably today," said Tom Grimmer, a spokesman at Peregrine Capital Ltd, one of the joint global coordinators of the issue.
Grimmer said 1.2 million applications had been printed and dozens of banks in the territory were delivering the forms.
Investors snapped up the initial 400,000 forms on Tuesday. A further 500,000 were printed overnight and soon exhausted on Wednesday.
The Hong Kong offering is expected to be more than 1,000 times oversubscribed, the highest ever in the territory.
Now many investors, after receiving the application forms, were standing in different lines.

"The queue is still there. They are not queuing for the forms but to buy bank drafts to subscribe the shares," a staff member at a Chinese bank in the Causeway Bay district told a customer who had waited for an hour to make an ordinary deposit.
The red-chip frenzy seems to have rattled Hong Kong's securities regulators and stock exchange.

The Securities and Futures Commission and the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong on Wednesday jointly said they were concerned about recent unusual price and volume movements in some shares, and warned they would take all necessary action to prevent abuses.
And on Thursday, the two agencies announced procedures for allocating shares in initial public offerings aimed at reducing the incentive for investors to apply for huge amounts of stock.
But analysts said demand for China-related red chips was not likely to cool with all of Hong Kong focused on the territory's impending reversion to China at midnight of June 30.
"I believe the fever is not over yet and it will extend to further for another 12 months in view of the continuous flowing of (foreign) funds into Hong Kong," Au-Young said.
"Demand varies from time to time and from sector to sector," said Andrew Zhou, vice-chairman of Chu Kong Shipping Development Co Ltd, a red chip whose shares will start trading on Friday.
"Today it is red chips, tomorrow it will be blue chips," he said."
